absent: Completion waiter sleep and wake semantics for stop and hotplug threads.
Timekeeping handover and reclamation reporting contracts during offline and starting.
Inter-processor queue linkage, signal delivery and remote handler dispatch loop.
Online, present, possible, bootable and housekeeping mask maintenance and SMT topology.
Hotplug callback registry, step names, rollback guarantees and sync-state update.
Stopper thread lifecycle, parking, work execution and mutual exclusion with offlining.
Idle thread allocation, stack reset, scheduler and RCU integration on bringup.

findings.text: SMP single-target remote invocation is offered as a public helper accepting a target identifier, a callback, opaque context and a synchronous wait selector, forwarding to an internal helper with no alternate mask.
Single-processor build offers the same single-target name with local-only semantics: non-zero targets are refused, otherwise the callback runs on the caller with interrupts masked across the call.

Hotplug teardown and bringup are exposed through device wrappers and explicit add and remove helpers plus shutdown of secondaries, hibernate resume assist, boot-time secondary bringup, starting notification, idle-online completion, idle-dead reporting and stopper unpark.

Stop coordination completion is reference counted: each participant signals once and only the final signal completes the shared waiter, while queued stop requests accumulate at the tail of the per-processor list in arrival order.

Single-call descriptor storage depends on wait mode: synchronous callers use caller-stack storage, asynchronous callers use a per-processor slot that must be locked before use, with debug builds optionally selecting the target slot by identifier.

The caller disables preemption across target selection and validity inspection and dispatch, preventing migration and concurrent offlining from missing wakeups; synchronous stack storage allows re-enabling preemption before blocking for completion to lower latency.

Dispatch to the calling processor runs inline: the descriptor is marked for debug tracking, released early, then invoked with interrupts masked before clearing the tracking marker; remote dispatch validates range and online status, releasing and failing when invalid, otherwise queueing for a signal.

Hotplug down refuses to offline the last online processor and unknown present identifiers, preserves at least one housekeeping domain member, and records frozen task state before state changes; up refuses unknown possible identifiers, unprepared nodes, disabled control and non-bootable targets.

Mask-guided target selection prefers the caller when already included, otherwise picks a nearby candidate by locality; callback execution is bracketed by entry and exit trace observations without altering functional behavior.

Debug tracking publishes callback identity before publishing the active descriptor pointer with release ordering, and clears the pointer with release ordering on completion, allowing remote diagnosers to pair non-null pointers with matching identity or order null after prior completion.

Cross-call serialization uses a flag in descriptor state observed with acquire semantics until clear; a debug variant may emit diagnostics while spinning, while the fast variant spins silently, both ending with an acquire barrier before the caller proceeds.

Acquisition pairs a wait for clear with an atomic claim in debug mode or a plain claim after waiting in normal mode, followed by a write barrier before other descriptor members are published; release requires the flag to be set and clears all state with release semantics.

Hotplug control nests an outer maps mutex around an inner write lock for state mutation, with device wrappers adding an outer device-hotplug mutex; inline and single-processor execution masks interrupts across the callback, and debug waiting holds preemption disabled.

Stop coordination exposes a pending counter with a waiter, and a stopper exposes a work list plus an enabled marker and a thread handle; call descriptors expose callback, context, type and destination with a lock flag and queue linkage.

Per-processor hotplug state exposes current state, desired target and frozen task indication, manipulated through per-processor accessors; device operations address processors by numeric identifier carried in generic device objects.

Teardown moves from running states toward offline through a teardown boundary: above the boundary the application processor thread is kicked and awaited, below it direct callbacks run, with failure resetting to the prior state and re-driving upward or warning when already dead.

Bringup moves from offline toward online through a bringup boundary: above the boundary the application thread is kicked, below it direct callbacks run up to a capped target, while starting notification runs a non-failing prefix and idle-online completion acts only on the expected idle state.

Idle-dead reporting advances from offline to idle-dead after timekeeping handover and reclamation reporting, delegating final completion to a surviving online processor rather than completing locally.

Parallel boot bringup optionally runs in two sweeps to a kick intermediate and then to online, handling threading primaries first and secondaries second, falling back to fully serialized bringup when disabled or unsupported.
Remote invocation entries are the synchronous-or-not single-target helper and its internal mask-aware form plus the descriptor-type-to-processor resolver used by diagnostics.

Hotplug control entries are device up and down, explicit add and remove, maps-locked and unlocked down and up, shutdown of secondaries, hibernate assist, nonboot bringup, starting notification and idle-online completion.

Invoking the cross-call helper with interrupts masked on an online caller, or from outside task context, risks deadlock and is diagnosed with one-time warnings; removal is excluded by holding preemption across the online inspection and signal queueing.

Stuck descriptor detection uses escalating timeouts scaled by online population, distinguishes backward clocks from genuine stalls, dumps remote task and local stack on first observation, re-sends the signal when no progress marker is visible, tracks stuck count, and can abort when a stall exceeds a configured panic threshold.

Shutdown demands that only the reboot survivor remain online and then permanently increments the disabled nesting count; down-path failures after partial progress warn when dead callbacks err, and an invalid diagnostic processor identifier is clamped for safe inspection.
Remote dispatch to an out-of-range or offline target, and single-processor dispatch to any non-zero target, fail with a device-absent error.

Hotplug refusal errors are distinct: last online or disabled control reports busy, unknown present or possible identity reports invalid argument, administratively prohibited offlining reports operation not supported, and non-bootable targets report permission denied.

Teardown without architecture support is represented by a null hook, parallel bringup defaults to enabled behind a read-only-after-init flag with a boolean boot parameter, and the weak architecture gate defaults to allowing parallel bringup.
